I'm split on this. I am fine with the change in general, but it does mean we're losing quite a few features that RTD has:
- safe and easy PR previews
- multiple versions support (for going back to older versions, or referencing the released version compared to the one on `main`)

Similarly, this means we're changing the url of the documentation, and since we do have quite a few users now we need to figure out how to forward people to the new url (if that is possible), or how to make sure people notice that the url changed and there are no new updates to the old one.

I've seen other projects work around github pages not supporting PR previews, but most of the time they were either very complex, very unsafe, or involved a separate hosting provider. However, I am not an expert on github pages so I might be missing something. For reference, the other libraries (like `healpix-resample`) do upload the built artifact in CI, but to get a working preview I have to find the artifact through several menus, download, unpack and start a local webserver. That's a significant DX downgrade compared to the single click we have with RTD.

Am I correct in assuming that you don't actually care about this being built using github-pages, but rather that we have a unified URL scheme for all projects? If so, I can try to check with @j34ni how we can best get this to work.

I'm sorry, but this kind of workflow makes it almost impossible to reasonably review PRs (the PR you proposed has 1.5k changed lines on different topics). As such, I think this actually does introduce a complex branching model, so the development workflow gets a hard -1 from me.

While I get what you're trying to do (have access to the changes before the land on main) and I have used this technique myself, let me remind you that merging github PRs is the same as just calling `git merge` in a separate branch, so you can just get the same effect by creating the integration branch on your own fork.

Also, having a single branch on the main repo won't work in all cases, even if the individual PRs remain open: that way we'll definitely run into merge conflicts. Or in other words, the branch would just be your own personal integration branch on the main repo, which I think is better off living on your personal fork (that's the point of forking)

### Claude sonnet review notes

I went through the diff and independently re-verified the correctness/performance claims made in this PR description. Summary of what I could and couldn't confirm:

**Verified**
- Implementation logic matches the description: `AUTO_PARALLEL_THRESHOLD = 32_768`, the `nthreads` branching (sequential / global Rayon pool / explicit pool), and `write_neighbours` (writes `-1` into fixed slots via `MainWind` keys, no compaction) all match `rust/healpix-geo-core/src/vectorized/nested/hierarchy.rs` and `scalar/nested/hierarchy.rs`.
- Cross-checked the topology invariant test (`valid_full_count == 6` at depth 0, `7 or 8` otherwise) independently using `healpy.get_all_neighbours` (nside 1/2/4) — matches exactly.
- Cross-checked the `cell=42, depth=2` example test values (`[111, -1, 21, 23, 43, 41, 40, 109]`, direction order SW,W,NW,N,NE,E,SE,S) against `healpy` directly — matches exactly, including the edge-only subset.
- Confirmed `12 * (4^0 + ... + 4^6) = 65,532`, matching the "all cells at depths 0–6" correctness-testing claim.
- Recomputed all four speedup ratios in the Performance table from the raw ms values: 7.8x / 3.3x / 11.9x / 6.9x all check out.

**Not verified (and why)**
- Did not run `cargo test` / `pytest` locally to reproduce the "Rust core: 80 passed" / "Python: 365 passed, 6 skipped" numbers. The crate requires `edition = "2024"` (rustc ≥ 1.87 via `cdshealpix`'s manifest), and only rustc 1.75 (Ubuntu apt) was available in my sandbox with no network path to a newer official toolchain — build failed at the manifest-parsing stage. Relying on GitHub Actions CI for this instead.
- Did not reproduce the absolute benchmark numbers (macOS 26.4 arm64, release build) — no matching hardware/OS available; only checked internal arithmetic consistency of the reported table, not the real wall-clock times.

No correctness issues found in the code itself. Recommend merging once CI is green.

self-review: 
- Added `cone_coverage_many` to `docs/api/nested.rst`.
- Clarified in the Python docstring that the eight-thread limit is an intentional conservative upper bound and that larger values are clamped.
- Added a short Rust comment explaining the reason for the conservative limit.


I also left the benchmark as a manually runnable script rather than adding it to CI, since benchmark CI integration is not required for this PR.

A small clarification regarding vectorization: `face_neighbour_transform` intentionally accepts a single face/direction pair because the transform is constant for each pair and there are only 12 × 8 possible combinations. Downstream callers such as `healpix-analyse` should obtain the transform once per touched face/direction and apply it to vectorized coordinate arrays. The cell-heavy operations, `pix2xyf` and `xyf2pix`, remain fully vectorized.

the output of `cdshealpix::nested::Layer::kth_neighbours` (and thus `healpix_geo`'s various `kth_neighbours` functions) follows a fixed order of S → W → N → E, so for `ring=1` the corner-neighbours are at `[0, 2, 4, 6]`, and the edge neighbours are at `[1, 3, 5, 7]` (though this is only guaranteed for the non-singularity pixels). I guess this information should probably be added to the docs.

I'm not opposed to adding a function that only returns specific immediate neighbours (cardinal directions only really make sense for the immediate neighbours), but note that if you're fetching both the two calls will always be less efficient than fetching all of them together.

Went with `level` on this last pass... The low-level statics keep `depth` since they mirror cdshealpix. ---

For the numbered items:

> toScheme: this is tricky. In https://github.com/GRID4EARTH/healpix-geo/pull/236 I've added a additional level parameter to the function that allows specifying the refinement levels, but only if we convert to a scheme that encodes the level in the cell ids 

 1. **`toScheme(cell, scheme, level?)`** mirrors #236's `convert`: `level` is accepted only when the target scheme encodes it in the id (`zuniq` today) and overrides the level the cell is read and encoded at; anywhere else it's a catchable `Error` — including level-overridden nested↔ring hops, which python's `convert` can express because it returns `(ids, levels)` while `toScheme` returns bare ids. Extending to `nuniq` / `mortie` should be mechanical.

 2. **`Ellipsoid.from` / prolate**: kept invalid — no consumer needs `b > a` and the authalic machinery is only exercised oblate (your "oblate" describes the prolate case; oblate/WGS84 is what already works). One-line lift once a use case shows. Agreed `inverse_flattening: 0` is a separate day.

 3. Gone - only the vectorized names now

 4. **`vertex` u/v**: strict `[0, 1]`, check folded into `spherical_vertex` per your inline comment, no unchecked variant. **That makes it a behavior change to the existing statics too**: their `vertex` now throws on out-of-`[0,1]` offsets, where `u = 1.5` previously returned the neighbouring cell's vertex (or trapped further out). `.d.ts` unchanged; yours to accept or reject — say the word if the statics should keep addressing neighbours and only `Grid` be strict. Scope note: the *offsets* are validated; the cell id beside them still traps on bad values (upstream, unchanged — `Grid` is the fully validated surface). Extending id validation to the statics is a willing follow-up.

 5. **vitest typechecking: adopted; it replaces `tsc --noEmit` here.** The string-assertion test became `types.test-d.ts` with `expectTypeOf`, dropping the `node:fs` import and with it **`@types/node`**; `typecheck.enabled` makes plain `vitest` run the check, so CI is unchanged. Verified: a planted type error in a runtime test file fails the run and `@ts-expect-error` still works — nothing tsc covered is lost, so the `typecheck` script is deleted (`typescript` stays; the checker shells out to it). Caveat: vitest calls the feature experimental and suggests pinning it; the lockfile does.

---

> (right now only zuniq, but I've had the request to also add nuniq, and maybe your own indexing scheme... if I remember correctly, that was called mortie?)

@keewis I'll take you up on a follow-up PR after this lands: an id-codec over nested — base-cell digit plus a base-4 path, level-encoding like zuniq — with the word format documented [here](https://github.com/espg/mortie/blob/main/docs/specification.md) and [here](https://github.com/espg/mortie/blob/main/docs/morton_index_datatype.md). On the order of 100–200 lines of dependency-free bit math plus golden vectors generated from mortie, and `toScheme`'s `level` parameter applies to it exactly as to zuniq.

One thing I realized from looking this over is that we should also be doing authalic coords in mortie, so starting to move that over too. Should make it easier to ride along on your gridlook PR once that + this lands!

Thanks for the thorough review @keewis — appreciate the quick turnaround on your end! Everything is folded into the rebuilt stack, same three commits, each green on its own.

On the `vertices` allocation question: in the sustained benchmark the bulk path stays flat (~1 ms/call, ~5 MB heap) over 60 rounds versus the scalar path degrading 80×, so the per-call `Float64Array` isn't a bottleneck — deferring `verticesInto` / multi-cell `vertices` until a real consumer shows pressure makes sense.

Beyond your comments, an adversarial review pass from claude found the stated "misuse throws a catchable `Error`" contract was false for the coordinate-taking methods: `lonLatToHealpix` / `cellsAt` forwarded into a cdshealpix assert, so one `NaN` in a buffer trapped the instance (`RuntimeError: unreachable`); same hole in `vertex` for far-out-of-range `u`/`v`. And the `u32` params were silently ToUint32-coerced (`bitCombine(2**32, 0)` arrived as `(0, 0)`). All of these now throw with the offending index named, with tests.

Five things came up while updating this that you should confirm or correct:

 1. **`toScheme` zuniq semantics** — converting *to* zuniq encodes the grid's depth; *from* zuniq uses the id's embedded depth (matching `vertex`); zuniq→zuniq is identity. Happy to re-encode at grid depth or reject mismatches instead.
 2. **`Ellipsoid.from` now validates**: positive finite axes, `semi_minor_axis <= semi_major_axis`, `inverse_flattening > 1`. Notably `inverse_flattening: 0` is rejected (it read like "a sphere" but produced `flattening: Infinity`) with a message pointing at `{ radius }`. And `EllipsoidInput` now type-checks the documented extra keys (fresh-literal tests, so the type is actually exercised).
 3. **Naming**: scalars now follow the python bindings but the bulk pair is still `centers` / `cellsAt` — we can rename to a plural convention if you have one you'd prefer.
 4. **`vertex`'s `u`/`v` bound is on the projected coordinate** (`-2 ≤ y ≤ 2`), not a hard `[0, 1]` clamp — offsets addressing neighbouring cells keep working; only the trapping cases throw. Tighten to cell-local if you'd rather the contract be strict.
 5. **`@types/node` rode along with `typescript`** (types-only; the `.d.ts` assertion test imports `node:fs`). Fine, or would you rather the test avoid node APIs?

> I would go with level, however: refinement_level is a lot to type, and unlike the CF conventions or the zarr dggs convention we will never have to worry about confusion with other types of levels (e.g. processing level).

I don't have strong opinion on `level` vs. `refinement_level`. I guess it might be OK for using either one or the other in each library, so using `level` here may be fine. In `legacy_converters` I'd prefer to stick with `refinement_level`, though, as I plan to reuse the same class (pydantic model) for both the conversion settings and the output metadata (Zarr DGGS convention).

I wouldn't alias parameters either, unless it is for the purpose of a deprecation cycle (which means the alias is temporary).

`healpix-geo` has existed for more than a year now, and we've kinda advertised it as the geoscience healpix package, so I'd be a bit more cautious with something as central as the `depth` parameter (but we can make the transition period 1-2 releases).

I would go with `level`, however: `refinement_level` is a lot to type, and unlike the CF conventions or the zarr dggs convention we will never have to worry about confusion with other types of levels (e.g. processing level).

I totally understand the initial motivation of using `depth` as healpix-geo development started as a cdshealpix-python extension or alternative. That said, I agree that renaming it to `refinement_level` would probably be the best way forward now, given that:

- IIUC `healpix-geo` depends on the `cdshealpix` rust crate but not on the `cdshealpix-python` package
- `healpix-geo` provides a Python package that is within the geospatial and grid4earth ecosystems, where `refinement_level` becomes usual (e.g., CF HEALPix conventions, Zarr DGGS conventions, I use it also in https://github.com/EOPF-DGGS/legacy-converters/pull/23). 
- we should probably prioritize consistency on the user side rather than on internals.

I'm -1 on a `level` alias. It doesn't bring much more convenience but introduces much API clutter. I'd keep aliases only for backward compatibility purpose.

I'm not sure how much healpix-geo is used in the wild, but given the young development stage I think it is OK to have a very short deprecation cycle or even no such cycle.

If I understand the plotting code correctly, what it does is:

1. define a target grid in lon / lat space (equirectangular projection)
2. find the cells closest to each target grid point
4. index the data to perform nearest-neighbour interpolation
5. use the standard `cartopy` / `matplotlib` functionality to plot

All but step 2 are independent of the DGGS, so it should be possible to generalize this to other DGGS, as well.

Just to make sure were talking about the same thing, here's how I understood what you said:

- model will keep using a spherical reference body
- observations will stay on an ellipsoidal surface

And both are on geographic coordinates. To compare, you're proposing to transform the latitudes from ellipsoidal-geographic to spherical-geographic (or inverse) by assuming spherical-geographic = authalic.

This would retain the equal-area properties for healpix, _but_ you'd be changing surface area by changing the assumed earth radius when going from spherical-geographic to authalic (the standard mean earth radius is ~6371000 m, while the authalic radius for WGS84 is 6371007.18m, so there's about a 7m difference that results in a small scaling factor for the area of every healpix cell). Afterwards the transformation is the same as what we use to extend healpix to ellipsoidal.

I'm not sure what this does with the data, and would this affect the healpix cell ids at all? That's something we're planning to evaluate, but another option that we've been considering is to represent the observation data as spline coefficents per cell, which would make interpolation (and thus the comparison) a lot easier. as a continuation of the discussion in #30:

by @d70-t:
> @pablo-richard, my thinking was about having model data on the same grid as observation data:
>
> Most (all?) global earth system models I know assume the planet to be a sphere, and run their simulations on the sphere. Lately, quite a few such models started to write their output to the healpix grid. For this mapping, they naturally use the latitude / longitude values of the sphere and apply the healpix pixelization without thinking about geographic / authalic etc...
>
> Now, of course people like to compare model results to actual observations of the planet. To do so, those people who are using both, the model output and the observational data need to:
> * find out which latitude on the (model-) sphere corresponds to which latitude of the (real-world) ellipsoid
> * bring both datasets on the same grid
> 
> To find out which model-latitude corrsponds to which real-world-latitude, I think the best option is to use exactly what people did during the initialization phase of the model. In many cases (at least IFS and ICON) this initialization will be based on ERA5, which uses geographic latitude. We've also confirmed that people running NICAM model do the same. 👉 for most (all?) ESM outputs, we want to interpret their (spherical) latitude as geographic latitude when comparing with real world data. Thus, it seems useful to only have geographic latitudes when storing them as numbers (as @keewis wrote), to avoid mixing things up.
> 
> This brings us to the second problem: having both datasets on the same grid. While ERA5 itself (so far...) doesn't live on healpix, it still (kind-of) defines the healpix grid which is used by ESM-models, and that's the grid defined by geographic latitude. If now all the observational datasets end up on *another* healpix grid, defined by authalic latitudes (even though expressed as geographic latitudes), the cells of the healpix grid will be at different positions, thus requiring remapping between models and observations. I think this is a hard-to-solve conflict, and I don't know what best to do. I think there are three bad options:
> 
> * model on **geographic** healpix, observatios on **authalic** healpix (both are equal-area on their natural grid, so this seems to be the best choice for each domain, but cross-domain operations will be painful)
> * model on **authalic** healpix, observations on **authalic** healpix (this seems to be the proper thing to do when talking about the real earth, but as models don't know about ellipsoids, doing this authalic-conversion will be super weird and will likely be done wrong in many cases. also the grid won't be equal-area anymore for the models...)
> * model on **geographic** healpix, observatios on **geographic** healpix (this is the reverse of the second, however: observation people know about ellipsoids and probably won't screw it up, however, the healpix grid wouldn't be equal area for observatiosn)
>
> Maybe this place is not the right one to discuss this, but we should do at some point and probably with a large community. My guess would be, that we'll end up with the first option if we don't coordinate early on, but it will be a pain in the long run. The two other options are both less perfect in their properties, but if we can agree on something in a large community, we might have much more fun in the long run when working with the data, because we don't have to regrid the data all the time.
>
> PS: I'm not that sure anymore, how to think of equal area in terms of the models... maybe we should actually think of the ellipsoid before doing model-averages...
